title: Symmetry Classification of Non-Reciprocal Responses in Multiterminal Ring Devices
abstract: We present a symmetry-based framework to classify the non-reciprocal responses of multiterminal ring quantum devices. The device is modeled as a ring of $n$ vertices, where a binary variable $e_k\in\{+1,-1\}$ on each bond encodes the preferred direction of signal flow between terminals. Non-reciprocity corresponds to a preferred current configuration on the ring, and the symmetry group of the device partitions all $2^n$ configurations into equivalence classes(orbits) characterized by a topological winding number $W$. Using the minimal non-trivial case $n=3$, we establish two results independent of microscopic details. First, lifting the degeneracy within an orbit generates non-reciprocal responses. For $n=3$ this requires simultaneous breaking of both time-reversal $T$ and spatial inversion $I$. Breaking either alone is insufficient. Second, the residual geometry symmetry after $T$ and $I$ are broken determines which responses are observable. For an isosceles triangular geometry, only two types of response are allowed: uniform circulation (all bonds carrying current in the same direction) and semi-circulation with the reversed bond on the geometrically distinct base. Semi-circulation with the reversed bond on either equal leg is symmetry-forbidden. Both predictions are validated using a minimal toy model of three quantum dots coupled to superconducting baths, which demonstrates a reactive quantum circulator response.
summary: This paper establishes a rigorous symmetry framework using group theory to classify non-reciprocal responses in multi-terminal quantum ring devices. By analyzing the constraints imposed by symmetries like time-reversal and inversion, it predicts that only specific circulation patterns are physically observable in real systems. The findings are validated through detailed calculations on a superconducting quantum dot model.
main_problem: The paper develops a symmetry-based framework to systematically classify non-reciprocal electrical responses occurring in multi-terminal quantum ring devices.
main_result: For an isosceles $n=3$ ring, the analysis predicts that only two types of non-reciprocal responses (uniform circulation and specific semi-circulation) are allowed due to residual geometric symmetries after breaking time-reversal ($T$) and inversion ($I$).
method: The core method involves applying group theory (Burnside's Lemma) to classify the $2^n$ bond configurations into symmetry orbits, linking topological invariants like the winding number ($W$) to observable physical responses.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as an $n$-vertex quantum ring device, analyzed using a minimal toy model of three quantum dots coupled to superconducting baths. The analysis extends from general ring structures to specific geometries like equilateral and isosceles triangles.
key_observables: Non-reciprocal transmission ($S_{nr}^{ab}$), the imaginary part of the current-current response function ($	ext{Im}[\chi_{nr}]$), and the absolute non-reciprocal weight ($R_{nr}^{tot}$).
important_parameters: The number of vertices $n$ (especially $n=3$), geometric symmetry type (equilateral vs. isosceles), and external field parameters like Zeeman fields ($\lambda$) or superconducting phase biases.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the applicability of group theory to classify configurations, assuming that non-reciprocity requires the simultaneous breaking of both time-reversal ($T$) and spatial inversion ($I$) symmetries.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the ring structure, show energy spectra splitting due to external fields, plot the reactive part of $	ext{Im}[\chi_{nr}]$ revealing distinct circulator/semi-circulator bands, and map out topological phase diagrams based on symmetry breaking.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general group theory framework for $n$-rings, then applying this to the minimal $n=3$ case, distinguishing between equilateral and isosceles geometries. It validates these theoretical predictions using a detailed quantum dot toy model calculation of linear response functions.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, abstract mathematical tool (symmetry classification) to predict observable transport phenomena in mesoscopic superconducting circuits, which is highly relevant for designing novel quantum devices.
